description: I am interested in space, science, data, and technology. I want to work on the Flame in Freefall challenge using NASA microgravity combustion data. I have interests in AI/ML, data analysis, research, and visualization. I am looking for teammates skilled in coding, AI/ML, statistics, astrophysics, UI/UX, or communication who can bring new ideas and work together to build a meaningful NASA Space Apps project.
summary: SPARK is an SI-powered web dashboard that turns two decades of NASA microgravity combustion experiments into ranked, cited fire-safety evidence for crewed spacecraft, space stations, Moon and Mars bases, and pressurized rovers. We normalized all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, covering 2,123 experiment runs from 22 tables and 352 reports, into one consistent dataset. A user picks a habitat and SPARK ranks every investigation with a transparent six-factor score they can re-weight. It maps every test's oxygen, pressure and airflow against habitat atmospheres, compares studies side by side, and answers plain-language questions with Google Gemini, using only retrieved NASA evidence and citing the report and page. The data reveals a critical gap: no PSI test was run inside the planned Moon-base atmosphere (30–34 % O₂ at less than or equal to 10.2 psi), and no solid cabin material was burned above 22.2 % O₂. SPARK makes that evidence easy to find, compare and interpret. Researchers can download the normalized data as CSV or JSON for predictive flammability modeling, and engineers can see what it means for detectors, suppression and material screening, so the next giant leap is a safer one.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPARK (Space Fire Atlas) helps professors, students, aerospace researchers and engineers answer one question: which NASA fire research matters for the habitat I'm designing, and what does it tell me?

• Missions: choose the ISS, a deep-space spacecraft, a Moon base, a pressurized rover, a Mars base or a spacesuit. All 24 PSI combustion investigations are ranked by a transparent score with six factors: atmosphere match, fire-safety focus (prevention, detection, suppression), material realism, fire scale, airflow match and data availability. Sliders re-weight it live, a stacked chart shows what drives each result, and studies never tested at the habitat's oxygen level are flagged.

• Test Conditions: every test plotted by oxygen and pressure against habitat design ranges, plus a density heatmap, an airflow chart and a FLEX suppression map. It shows that no PSI test sits inside the Moon-base atmosphere.

• Investigations: filter by pillar, platform or hardware family (ACME/CIR, MDCA/CIR, MSG flow duct, Cygnus, smoke instruments). Each study has an AI summary, sourced key findings, charts of its own test runs, what varied and what was held constant, fuels and sample sizes, sensors, publications, its DOI, and a CSV/JSON download with a data dictionary.

• Compare: two to four investigations side by side, with oxygen and pressure ranges and an AI-written comparison.

• Ask SPARK: plain-language questions answered by Google Gemini using only retrieved PSI evidence (4,431 report passages). Each claim is cited, e.g. [PSI-25 p.12], and data gaps such as partial gravity are flagged.

• Insights: lessons from Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir and Artemis II; myths microgravity research overturned; implications for next-generation equipment (detectors, gas suppression, extinguishers, material screening, ventilation controls, fire models); data gaps for the Moon and Mars; and Earth applications such as water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter gear.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline downloads metadata, experimental tables and final reports from the public PSI repository. Twenty small parsers normalize 22 differently formatted tables into one schema, converting units and fixing source quirks. For example, "LOW O2" had been read as 2 % oxygen and "3400%" meant 34 %; every fix was traced to the original cell. A hand-curated catalog adds fire-safety pillars and key findings, each citing its NASA source. Report text is split into 4,431 searchable passages. A FastAPI service ranks investigations, runs BM25 search and asks Gemini for grounded answers. If the model is busy it falls back to a second model, and then to an evidence-only answer. A React dashboard (TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, Plotly) is served from Vercel with no login.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

• Turns an overwhelming archive into ranked, cited answers in seconds.

• Exposes the gaps that matter for Artemis-era habitats: oxygen-enriched cabin materials and partial gravity.

• Gives modelers clean, unit-consistent data for predictive flammability work.

• Links evidence to equipment design and to fire safety on Earth.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

• A transparent, adjustable ranking instead of a black-box score.

• A coverage map that turns missing data into an insight.

• AI that must cite NASA evidence, and says so when the evidence is missing.

FACTORS I CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty: nominal versus measured conditions are labelled, and inverse-flame oxygen is separated from room air. PSI holds no partial-gravity data, so microgravity and 1-g results are presented as bounds. Rocket and propellant fires are out of scope. Accessibility: colorblind-safe chart palette, legends and table views. No NASA branding is used in generated content.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, pypdf, httpx, FastAPI), TypeScript/React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Plotly, Google Gemini API, Vercel, draw.io.
